name: Film and TV trivia (medium)
description: 50 medium questions about films, television, animation, actors, directors, from any decade. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: In Citizen Kane, what does the dying Charles Foster Kane's last word, "Rosebud", turn out to refer to?
items.explain: The film's closing shots show Kane's childhood sled, with "Rosebud" painted on it, being thrown into a furnace.

items.question: Which newspaper magnate banned any mention of Citizen Kane in his papers when the film was released?
items.explain: On the film's release, Hearst prohibited any mention of it in his newspapers.

items.question: Who co-wrote Citizen Kane with Orson Welles?
items.explain: Citizen Kane was co-written by Welles and Herman J. Mankiewicz.

items.question: Which author wrote the 1959 novel on which Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho was based?
items.explain: Psycho (1960) was based on Robert Bloch's 1959 novel of the same name.

items.question: The 2017 documentary 78/52 takes its title from the number of camera setups and cuts in a famous scene from which Hitchcock film?
items.explain: The documentary examines Psycho's shower scene, which has 78 camera setups and 52 cuts.

items.question: Which composer wrote the shrieking string score for Psycho's shower scene, which Hitchcock first wanted to leave without music?
items.explain: Bernard Herrmann's shrieking violins scored the scene, even though Hitchcock at first resisted using any soundtrack for it.

source.title: Psycho's Shower Scene: How Hitchcock Upped the Terror—and Fooled the Censors

items.question: What nickname did the Jaws crew give to the film's troublesome mechanical shark?
items.explain: The production nicknamed the malfunctioning mechanical great white "Bruce". Its breakdowns pushed Spielberg to keep it mostly hidden.

source.title: Jaws at 50: How the 1975 Steven Spielberg shark thriller became a commercial and cultural phenomenon - ABC News

items.question: Which composer created the ominous, minimalist theme that signals the shark's approach in Jaws?
items.explain: Because the mechanical sharks often malfunctioned, Spielberg relied on John Williams's minimalist theme to suggest the shark's presence.

items.question: Who wrote the 1974 novel on which the film Jaws was based?
items.explain: Jaws (1975) was based on Peter Benchley's 1974 novel.

items.question: Jaws was shot mostly on location at which Massachusetts island?
items.explain: Jaws was shot mostly on location at Martha's Vineyard, making it the first major motion picture shot on the ocean.

items.question: Who directed Casablanca and won the Academy Award for Best Director for it?
items.explain: Michael Curtiz directed Casablanca and was named Best Director for it.

items.question: Casablanca was loosely based on which unproduced stage play?
items.explain: The film was loosely based on Murray Burnett and Joan Alison's unproduced play Everybody Comes to Rick's.

items.question: Casablanca was nominated for eight Academy Awards. How many did it win?
items.explain: It won three: Best Picture, Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay.

items.question: Which 1960 American western was a remake of Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai?
items.explain: Seven Samurai was remade as John Sturges's western The Magnificent Seven in 1960.

items.question: Which actor, a frequent Kurosawa collaborator, starred in Seven Samurai alongside Takashi Shimura?
items.explain: Toshiro Mifune and Takashi Shimura were the film's leading men, both longtime Kurosawa collaborators.

items.question: Which Kurosawa film won the top prize at the 1951 Venice Film Festival and then an honorary Academy Award?
items.explain: Rashomon won the top prize at Venice in 1951 and an honorary Academy Award as the best foreign-language film, given before that category existed.

items.question: Which 2019 film became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture?
items.explain: Bong Joon-ho's Parasite was the first foreign-language film to win Best Picture, and also won the Palme d'Or at Cannes.

items.question: How many Academy Awards did Parasite win?
items.explain: It won four Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director, Best Original Screenplay and Best International Feature.

items.question: Who directed Parasite?
items.explain: Parasite was directed by Bong Joon-ho, who also co-wrote the screenplay.

items.question: Which 1988 Pixar short became the first computer-generated film to win an Academy Award?
items.explain: Tin Toy won the 1988 Academy Award for Animated Short Film and helped pave the way for Toy Story.

items.question: Which 1995 film was the first computer-animated feature film?
items.explain: Toy Story, released in 1995, was Pixar's debut feature and the first computer-animated feature film.

items.question: Which Pixar figure received a Special Achievement Academy Award for leading the Toy Story team?
items.explain: John Lasseter received a Special Achievement Academy Award for his leadership of the team that made the first feature-length computer-animated film.

items.question: Which singer-songwriter wrote the Academy Award-nominated song "You've Got a Friend in Me" for Toy Story?
items.explain: Randy Newman's song was one of Toy Story's three Academy Award nominations, alongside Best Original Score and Best Original Screenplay.

items.question: What derisive nickname did industry critics give Walt Disney's plan to make Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs?
items.explain: Critics called the plan "Disney's Folly", believing audiences would not sit through a full-length cartoon.

items.question: Walt Disney received an Honorary Academy Award for Snow White made up of one full-size statuette and how many miniature ones?
items.explain: The Honorary Academy Award given in 1939 consisted of one full-size statuette and seven miniature ones.

items.question: Who provided the voice of Snow White in Disney's 1937 film?
items.explain: Adriana Caselotti voiced Snow White in the 1937 film.

source.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)

items.question: At which festival did Spirited Away share the top prize in 2002, becoming the first animated feature to win it?
items.explain: Spirited Away was a co-recipient of the Golden Bear at the 2002 Berlin festival, the first animated feature to win the festival's highest prize.

source.title: Spirited Away Changed Animation Forever. Here's How

items.question: In Spirited Away, into what animals are Chihiro's parents turned after eating cursed food?
items.explain: Chihiro's parents are turned into pigs after eating cursed food, and she tries to save them.

source.title: 'Spirited Away' Broke Records and Made [Academy Award] History

items.question: Which Hayao Miyazaki film won Best Animated Feature at the 75th Academy Awards?
items.explain: Spirited Away won Best Animated Feature at the 75th Academy Awards, in the category's second year.

source.title: 'Spirited Away' Broke Records and Made [Academy Award] History

items.question: The Simpsons first appeared as animated shorts on which show before getting their own series?
items.explain: The Simpson family spent two years on The Tracey Ullman Show before their own series premiered on Fox on December 17, 1989.

items.question: Which Simpson family member's name was not taken from one of Matt Groening's real relatives?
items.explain: The other family members were named after Groening's relatives, but Bart's name is an anagram of "brat".

items.question: In the lobby of whose office did Matt Groening conceive the idea for The Simpsons?
items.explain: Groening sketched the Simpson family while waiting in the office of producer James L. Brooks.

items.question: Which composer did Matt Groening pick to write the iconic Simpsons theme tune?
items.explain: Groening chose Danny Elfman to compose the show's theme song.

source.title: Creating 'The Simpsons:' How Matt Groening's Own Family Inspired the Characters

items.question: In which US city is Breaking Bad set?
items.explain: Breaking Bad is set in Albuquerque, New Mexico, where chemistry teacher Walter White starts making meth.

items.question: Who created Breaking Bad?
items.explain: Breaking Bad was created and produced by Vince Gilligan for AMC.

items.question: What alias does Walter White adopt in Breaking Bad's drug trade?
items.explain: Walter Hartwell White is also known by his alias Heisenberg.

items.question: Who created the HBO crime drama The Sopranos?
items.explain: The Sopranos was created by David Chase for HBO and ran for six seasons.

items.question: Which 2021 film, co-written by David Chase, is a prequel to The Sopranos?
items.explain: The Many Saints of Newark was the 2021 prequel film to The Sopranos, co-written by Chase.

source.title: 'The Sopranos' Creator Sets First Series at HBO Since Groundbreaking Mafia Classic

items.question: In which year did The Sopranos begin broadcasting on HBO?
items.explain: The series was greenlit in 1997 but was first broadcast on HBO on January 10, 1999.

items.question: Which actor played the First Doctor in the original run of Doctor Who?
items.explain: William Hartnell played the First Doctor in the show's first serial, An Unearthly Child, in 1963.

items.question: Which writer scripted the 1963 Doctor Who serial that introduced the Daleks?
items.explain: The Daleks serial, first broadcast in December 1963, was written by Terry Nation.

items.question: Who, the BBC drama department's first female producer, led production of the first Doctor Who serial?
items.explain: Verity Lambert, the BBC drama department's first female producer, led production of An Unearthly Child.

items.question: Why was the first episode of Doctor Who repeated the week after its debut?
answers: The BBC had broadcast the wrong episode
A recording fault spoiled the original transmission
Viewers were distracted by news of Kennedy's assassination
A strike disrupted the BBC's schedule that week
items.correct: Viewers were distracted by news of Kennedy's assassination
items.explain: The first episode aired the day after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, so it was repeated the following week.

items.question: Which star of M*A*S*H also directed its two-and-a-half-hour series finale, "Goodbye, Farewell, and Amen"?
items.explain: Alan Alda, who played Hawkeye Pierce, directed the finale, which first aired on February 28, 1983.

items.question: In M*A*S*H, what is the number of the Mobile Army Surgical Hospital unit at the centre of the story?
items.explain: The series follows the staff of the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War.

items.question: What is the hometown of M*A*S*H's Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce?
items.explain: Hawkeye Pierce's hometown is listed as Crabapple Cove, Maine.

items.question: John Cleese and Connie Booth conceived Fawlty Towers after staying at a hotel in which English seaside town?
items.explain: The idea came from a stay at a Torquay hotel, whose rude owner, Donald Sinclair, inspired the character of Basil.

items.question: Who co-created and co-wrote Fawlty Towers with John Cleese?
items.explain: Fawlty Towers was created by John Cleese and Connie Booth, who also played the chambermaid Polly.

items.question: Which actor played the hapless Spanish waiter Manuel in Fawlty Towers?
items.explain: Andrew Sachs played Manuel, the kind but often confused waiter at the hotel.

items.question: Fawlty Towers was inspired by a 1970 stay at a Torquay hotel by which comedy troupe?
items.explain: Monty Python stayed at the Gleneagles Hotel in Torquay in May 1970, and Cleese and Booth stayed on after filming finished.
